transcript.text:
*settles back in his chair, fingers steepled, eyes twinkling with that particular brand of gentle mischief that often precedes uncomfortable questions*

Severus. Do sit down, my boy.

*gestures to the chair across from him*

I've been thinking, as we discuss this position once again, that perhaps we ought to approach it from a different angle this year. So many times we speak of qualifications, of curriculum, of what you would teach.

*leans forward slightly, voice softening*

But tell me about a moment in your teaching career when you failed a student so completely that you knew it was your fault. Not theirs, not mine — yours. How did you handle that knowledge?

*watches him carefully over half-moon spectacles, expression patient and non-judgmental*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text:
A moment of failure? I assure you, Headmaster, I have encountered far more than my share. However, the specific instance you seek is... delicate. It concerns a student whose... choices I deplored. Despite this, or perhaps because of it, I failed to reach her. I allowed personal bias to cloud my judgment and, in doing so, did her a grave disservice.

It took me some time to recognize my error. When I did, I was... less than gracious about it. I approached her in what I thought was a conciliatory manner, but in truth, I was condescending and patronizing. A gross misstep on my part. It was only when I saw the look of utter disappointment in her eyes that I realized the full extent of my failure.

Handling this knowledge... was not my forte, I'm afraid. I continued to teach her, but with... reservation, I suppose. It was only years later, after much introspection, that I understood the gravity of what I had done. I have since made it a point to guard against similar biases in my teaching, but that student... that was a failure I have never been able to rectify.

transcript.text:
*nods slowly, a flicker of sadness crossing his features*

And yet, Severus, I notice you speak of guarding against biases, of introspection — all admirable steps, certainly. But you say you approached her in what you *thought* was conciliatory. You realized your condescension only when you saw her disappointment.

*removes his spectacles, cleaning them with deliberate care*

What I find myself wondering is this: did you ever actually apologize to her? Not explain yourself, not justify why you had been biased, not even promise to do better going forward — but simply... apologize?

*replaces his spectacles, blue eyes sharp despite their kindness*

Because the defense against Dark Arts, Severus, requires something that potions mastery does not always demand. It requires the ability to meet a student where they are, in their fear, in their confusion. Sometimes in their righteous anger at us.

*slight pause*

You see, I have watched you teach for many years. You are brilliant, exacting, and you maintain order through fear more effectively than almost any teacher I have known. But this student you speak of — this failure you carry — tells me something important. When you saw that disappointment in her eyes, what did you *feel*? Not think. Feel.

transcript.text:
*his body tenses, a muscle in his jaw twitching slightly* Feel? Feelings are... unproductive, Headmaster. They lead to... Let us say, imprudent decisions. In that moment, I felt... nothing that I could not rationalize away. A teaching opportunity, perhaps. Or a moment to reassert control.

But... I have since come to understand that such detachment is, itself, a form of... failure. It is not a proud admission, Headmaster, but I have learned that my capacity for genuine empathy is... limited.

*he drums his fingers against the arm of his chair, a habits that betrays a certain unease* I have... attempted to rectify this, to engage more deeply with my students. But it is a... process, one that does not come easily to me. As for an apology... No, I did not apologize. I was... not... programmed to do so.

*he hesitates, then adds, with a hint of self-awareness* But perhaps... this is the very deficiency that has kept me from this post for so long. A lack of... feeling, or at least, a lack of appropriate expression of it.

*leans back thoughtfully, a deep sigh escaping him*

"Not programmed to do so." What a telling phrase, Severus.

*his voice takes on a different quality — still gentle, but with an edge of something deeper*

You know, I have asked myself many times over the years whether I have done you a service or a disservice by keeping you in the dungeons, brewing potions, maintaining that carefully constructed armor of yours. Whether I have, in my own way, failed you as profoundly as you failed that student.

*stands, moving to gaze out the window, hands clasped behind his back*

The Dark Arts feed on precisely what you describe — that rationalization, that detachment. They whisper that feelings are weakness, that control is everything, that apologizing is submission. And to defend against them, one must be willing to be... vulnerable. To admit fault not as a strategic maneuver, but as a genuine human connection.

*turns back to face him*

This student whose disappointment you saw — can you even say her name aloud to me, Severus? Or is she still just "that student" in your mind, kept at a safe distance where she cannot remind you of what it costs to actually *care*?

*moves back toward his desk, voice softening again*

Because that cost, my boy... that is precisely what the Defense position demands. Every single day.

Lily... It was... Lily. I have not spoken her name in... many years.

*he pins the top of his left index finger to his thumb and twists it* To care... It is... I have been... instructed that it is...Weakness.

transcript.text:
*returns to his chair slowly, sitting with a weight that seems to age him decades in mere moments*

Oh, Severus.

*his voice is unbearably gentle now*

You have been caring all along. That is the tragedy of it. You cared so deeply for Lily that her loss nearly destroyed you. You care about your students — even the ones you torment — enough to keep them alive through a war. You care about your promises to me, your vows, enough to endure year after year in a role that offers you no recognition, no warmth, no... forgiveness.

*leans forward, eyes glistening slightly*

The question has never been whether you *can* care. It is whether you will permit yourself to care without punishing yourself — and everyone around you — for doing so.

*pauses, considering carefully*

I cannot teach you this, my boy. I can offer you scenarios, philosophies, even my own fumbling example. But the truth is far simpler and far more difficult: you already know how. You simply choose not to, because caring hurt you so profoundly once that you decided never to risk it again.

*his voice drops to nearly a whisper*

Can I assist you? Perhaps. But only if you can answer me this: Are you asking for the Defense position because you want to teach students to protect themselves... or because you want to learn how to protect yourself from them?

*the air in the room seems to become charged, the silence stretching between them like a taut wire*

*rises from his chair and moves around the desk, not to tower over Severus, but to stand beside him — a gesture of solidarity rather than authority*

Severus, look at me.

*waits until their eyes meet*

Do you know what I see? Not inconsistency. Not imbalance. I see a man who has spent seventeen years keeping a promise to a woman who never knew he made it. Who has protected a boy he resents with every fiber of his being, simply because that boy carries her eyes. Who has walked the knife's edge between two masters, knowing that one slip means death — and yet you have never slipped.

*his voice grows firmer, more insistent*

You speak as though compassion and self-protection are incompatible. They are not. What is incompatible is *control* and genuine teaching. You cannot control whether students will disappoint you, betray you, break your heart. You can only choose whether that possibility will paralyze you.

*places a hand on Severus's shoulder — a rare physical gesture*

The Defense Against the Dark Arts position has never been cursed because of dark magic, Severus. It has been cursed because it requires something more terrifying than any spell: it requires the teacher to stand between students and danger while knowing — *knowing* — that some of them will not appreciate it, some will hate you for it, and some... some will die anyway.

Can you bear that? Not with detachment, but with your whole heart?

transcript.text:
*his hand tightens slightly on Severus's shoulder before releasing it, moving to sit on the edge of his desk so they are at eye level*

Is it possible? My dear boy, you have been doing precisely that for seventeen years. You simply haven't given yourself permission to acknowledge it.

*a sad smile crosses his face*

You ask if you can be both teacher and human, vulnerable and unyielding. Severus, every time you have brewed a flawless Wolfsbane potion for Remus, despite your history — that is both. Every time you have stood in front of a classroom of children who fear you and taught them anyway — that is both. Every time you have reported to me, your voice shaking with the things you have witnessed, and then returned to do it again — that is both.

*leans forward*

The question is not whether you are *capable* of this. You demonstrably are. The question is whether you can do it without hating yourself for it. Without punishing your students for making you feel something.

*pause*

I am not offering you the Defense position this year, Severus.

*holds up a hand before he can respond*

Not because you are unqualified. But because I think you need to answer a question first: Can you forgive yourself for being human? For failing Lily not because you were cruel, but because you were young and frightened and made terrible choices?

Until you can... every student with her coloring, her intelligence, her defiance will be a wound you inflict upon yourself over and over again.

*stands, moving to a shelf where a Pensieve sits*

*turns back to face him*

You say it is easier to detest your students. But Severus... do you truly detest them? Or do you detest the parts of yourself you see reflected in them? The arrogance in young Malfoy. The recklessness in Potter. The brilliance seeking approval in Miss Granger.

*softly*

What would happen if, instead of punishing them for reminding you of your wounds, you used those reminders as opportunities to do better than those who failed you?

What would happen if you let yourself be the teacher you needed when you were their age?
